column2: A sage, self-controlled, with anger conquered, master of belly and sex, always offering to the fires, restrained, attending to the twilight prayers,
who in this way, with many observances, eats by the month and lives under the open sky, his dwelling is declared.
Having gone to heaven in his own body, O king, like an immortal, he enjoys holy heaven as he wishes, by rule.
This, best of the Bharatas, is the supreme rule of sacrifices, explained in order, whose substance is the fruit of fasting.
Thus, Partha, poor men can obtain the fruit of sacrifice; having kept this fast, one may go to the highest goal, devoted to the worship of gods and the twice-born, O best of the Bharatas.
This rule of fasting has been told in detail for the self-controlled, the heedful, the pure and the great-souled,
for those turned from hypocrisy and malice, of resolved mind, steady and unshaken; let there be no doubt in you about this.
[Bhishma] All holy places are indeed virtuous for the wise; but hear from me attentively what is a tirtha and what is purity.
One should bathe in the mental tirtha, in the fathomless, clear, pure lake of steadfastness with the water of truth, holding to eternal goodness.
The purity of a tirtha is freedom from desire for gain, gentleness, truth, uprightness, non-harm to all beings, absence of cruelty, self-control and calm.
Those who are free of possessiveness, of ego, of dualities and of acquisition, who live on alms, are pure and are themselves tirthas.
One who knows the truth and has no thought of "I" is called the supreme tirtha. This is the mark of purity: seeing the same everywhere.
Those whose self has washed off passion, darkness and goodness are not attached to purity or impurity, and seek only their own task.
Delighting in renunciation, all-knowing and all-seeing, they are, by purity of conduct, the purity of purposes; they are holy places and pure.
One whose body is merely wet with water is not called bathed; he who has bathed in self-control is bathed, pure within and without.
Knowledge is the body's chief purity here, and so are having nothing of one's own and clarity of mind.
Purity of conduct, purity of mind and purity of tirtha are the highest good; the purity born of knowledge is held to be supreme.
Those who have bathed in the mental tirtha with the lamp of the mind and the power of knowledge of Brahman are the knowers who see the knower of the field.
One who always has purity laid upon him and is endowed with good, endowed only with virtues, is a man ever pure.
These tirthas within the body have been told, O Bharata; hear also of the holy tirthas on the earth.
As the parts of the body are made pure, so are the parts of the earth, and holy waters.
By prayer to a tirtha, by bathing and offering to the ancestors, they shake off sin at the tirthas and, purified, go happily to heaven.
By the acceptance of the good and by the earth's power, those places are exceedingly holy, and by the power of the water.
Other holy tirthas are of the mind and of the earth; one who has bathed in both soon attains perfection.
An act without strength, or strength without action, does not accomplish the aim here; only when joined does it succeed.
So, endowed with bodily purity and purity of tirtha, one then gains perfection; supreme is the twofold purity.
[Yudhishthira] By what conduct, O king of kings, do men living in the world attain the highest heaven, and how do they come to hell?
Having cast off the dead body like wood or clod, people go from here to the other world; who follows them?
[Bhishma] Here comes the blessed Brihaspati of noble mind; ask this very fortunate one this eternal secret.
No one else today can tell this; there is no speaker equal to Brihaspati anywhere.
[Vaishampayana] While those two, Partha, the son of the Ganga and Yudhishthira, were speaking so, the blessed Brihaspati of pure soul arrived.
Then the king, rising, with Dhritarashtra at the head, paid incomparable honour, and so did all the assembly.
Then the king, son of Dharma, of fair vows, approached the blessed Brihaspati and duly asked his question.
[Yudhishthira] Blessed one, knower of dharma, expert in all scriptures, who is a mortal's helper: father, mother, son, or teacher?
[Brihaspati] Born alone, O king of kings, a creature dies alone; alone he crosses hard places, and alone he goes to a bad end.
Father, mother, brother, son, teacher, and the circle of kin and of friends are no helpers.
Having cast off the dead body like wood or clod, people wait a moment and then turn away; when they have abandoned that body, dharma alone follows.
Therefore dharma should always be followed by men for help; a being joined with dharma does not go to hell.
So a wise man should follow dharma with wealth gained justly; dharma alone is a man's helper in the next world.
From greed, delusion, pity or fear, an ill-taught man does what should not be done for others' sake, bewildered by greed.
Dharma, wealth and desire are the triad that is the fruit of life; this triad is to be obtained free of unrighteousness.
[Yudhishthira] I have heard the blessed one's words, full of dharma and supremely good. I wish to know about the body's analysis.
When a being is dead, without body, subtle, gone to the unmanifest, beyond the range of the eye, how does dharma follow?
[Brihaspati] Earth, wind, space, water and fire as the fifth, together with intellect and the self, always see dharma.
They are the constant witnesses of all beings here, and with them dharma follows that living being.
Skin, bone, flesh, semen and blood, wise one, abandon the body when it is deprived of life.
Then, joined with dharma, that soul prospers happily here and hereafter. What more shall I tell you?
[Yudhishthira] The blessed one has shown how dharma follows. But I wish to know how semen comes about.
[Brihaspati] The gods who dwell in the body eat food, O lord of men: earth, wind, space, water, fire and mind.
When those five elements, with mind as sixth, are satisfied, O king, pure soul, great semen is produced.
Then at the union of woman and man, Partha, the embryo arises. All this is told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
[Yudhishthira] You have told how the embryo is formed. Tell what the man does when he is born.
[Brihaspati] Just as he arrives, he is overcome by those elements, and when released by them, he goes again to another state; joined to the elements, he indeed obtains life.
Then the five deities abiding in the elements watch his deeds, good or bad. What more do you wish to hear?
[Yudhishthira] Having left skin, bone and flesh, and deprived of those elements, where does the blessed soul abide, experiencing pleasure and pain?
[Brihaspati] The soul, joined with dharma, quickly becomes semen; reaching the woman's season, it is born in time, O Bharata.
A man meets torment and slaying by Yama's men, suffering and the wheel of rebirth, and torment.
And in this world, O king, that being from birth enjoys his own deed, relying on the fruit of dharma.
If from birth he follows dharma as he can, then, having become a man, he always enjoys happiness.
But if in between he follows unrighteousness, after happiness that soul meets sorrow.
Joined with unrighteousness, gone to Yama's realm, he suffers great pain and is born in an animal womb.
By what deed, and in what womb the soul here, joined with delusion, is born, hear me tell that.
What is said in the scripture, with the Itihasa, in the sacred verse: the mortal world enters Yama's terrible realm.
A twice-born who, having studied the four Vedas, is deluded and accepts gifts from a fallen man is born in the womb of a donkey.
A donkey lives fifteen years; dying, he becomes a bullock and lives seven years.
A bullock, dying, is born a brahmin-demon; as a brahmin-demon for three months, and then is born a brahmin.
One who has performed a sacrifice for a fallen man is born in the womb of a worm, and lives there fifteen years, O Bharata.
Released from being a worm, he is then born a donkey; a donkey for five years, a pig for five, a dog for one year, and then he is born a man.
The foolish pupil who does wrong to his teacher undergoes three rebirths here, without doubt.
First a dog, O king, then a flesh-eater, then a donkey, then a tormented ghost, and afterwards he is born a brahmin.
A sinful pupil who even in mind goes to his teacher's wife goes through the lower rebirths by his unrighteous thought here.
Born in a dog's womb he lives three years; dying there, he is born in a worm's womb.
Attaining the state of a worm he lives one year, and then, dying, is born in a brahmin's womb.
If a teacher kills a pupil like a son without cause, by his own wilfulness, he too is born a goose.
The son who despises his father or mother, that creature too, O king, dying, is first born a donkey.
A donkey for ten months, a dog for fourteen, a cat for seven months, and then he is born a man.
One who reviles mother and father is born a myna; having struck them, O king, he is born a tortoise.
A tortoise for ten years, a shakyaka for three, a serpent for six months, and then he is born a man.
One who eats his master's food yet serves what the king hates, deluded, dying is born a monkey.
A monkey for ten years, a mouse for three, a dog for six months, and then he is born a man.
A man who has stolen a deposit goes to Yama's realm, and after a hundred rebirths is born in a worm's womb.
He lives there fifteen years, O Bharata; when his evil deed is exhausted, he is born a man.
An envious man dying is born a Sharngaka bird; a man who betrays trust, ill-minded, is born a fish.
Having been a fish for eight years, O Bharata, he is born a deer; a deer for four months, then a goat.
A goat, dying after a full year, is then born an insect; as an insect he is then born a man.
One who steals grain, barley, sesame, black gram, horse gram, mustard, chickpeas, peas, green gram, wheat and flax,
or other crops, out of delusion, a senseless creature, is born, great king, a shameless mouse.
Then after death, great king, he is again born a pig, and the pig, as soon as born, dies of disease, O king.
Then by that deed the fool is born a dog, O king; having been a dog for five years, he is then born a man.
One who has violated another's wife is born a wolf, then a dog, jackal, vulture, serpent, heron and crane.
The ill-minded who in delusion assaults his brother's wife attains the state of a pungent lover for a year, O king.
One who, out of desire, assaults a friend's wife, a teacher's wife or a king's wife, dying, is born a pig.
A pig for five years, a dog-like creature for five, an ant for six months, an insect for a month; having passed through these rebirths, he is born in a worm's womb.
He lives thirteen months in a worm's womb; then, having exhausted his unrighteousness, he is born a man again.
One who in delusion obstructs a wedding, a gift or a sacrifice when it is at hand, dying, is born a worm.
A worm lives fifteen years, O Bharata; having exhausted his unrighteousness, he is then born a man.
One who has first given a maiden and gives her a second time, he too, O king, dying, is born in a worm's womb.
He lives there thirteen years, Yudhishthira; when his unrighteousness is exhausted, he is born a man.
One who has begun the rite for the gods and for the ancestors and eats without offering is born a crow.
A crow for ten years, then a cock, then a quail for a month, and from that a man.
One who despises his elder brother, equal to a father, dying, is born in a heron's womb.
A heron lives for ten, two, seven and five months; then, dying, he attains the state of a man.
A low-caste man who goes to a brahmin woman is born in a worm's womb; having begotten offspring there, he is then born a mouse.
An ungrateful man, O king, dying, goes to Yama's realm and there receives a dreadful beating from the angry ones.
The lance, the club, the spear, the terrible fire-pot, the sword-leaf forest, the burning sand, the false silk-cotton tree:
these and many other torments he reaches in Yama's realm, and having endured those fierce pains, he is slain, O Bharata.
Reaching the wheel of rebirth he is born in a worm's womb, a worm for fifteen years, O Bharata; then, reaching an embryo, the child dies there.
Then, born in many hundreds of wombs, and passing through many rebirths, he is then born an animal.
Dying, after suffering for many years here, joined to the state of no return, he is born a tortoise.
The lowest of men, armed, who kills an unarmed man, for gain or from enmity, dying is born a donkey.
A donkey lives two years and is then killed by a weapon; dying, he is born in a deer's womb, always in fear.
The deer is killed by a weapon after a year; the slain deer becomes a fish, which is caught in a net.
When the fourth month arrives, he is born a beast of prey; a beast of prey for ten years, a leopard for five.
Then, dying as driven by the turning of time, having exhausted his unrighteousness, he is born a man.
The ill-minded who has killed a woman goes to Yama's realm, meets many torments and twenty rebirths.
After that, great king, he is born in a worm's womb; a worm for twenty years, he is born a man.
A man who steals food is born a fly; for many months he is under the sway of flies; then, exhausting his sin, he gains human birth.
A man who steals an instrument is born a gnat; a man who steals food mixed with oilcake is born a dreadful mouse like a brown one.
One who steals salt is born a cricket; one who steals curds, a crane; one who steals unprepared fish, a water bird.
One who steals milk is born a crane; one who steals oil is born an oil-drinker; the ill-minded who steals honey is born a stinging insect.
The ill-minded who steals iron is born a crow; one who steals payasa attains the state of a partridge.
One who steals a flour cake is born a pot-owl; one who steals fruit or radish, or a cake, an ant.
The ill-minded who steals bronze is born a Harita bird; one who steals a silver vessel is born a pigeon.
A man who steals paints and perfumes, O king, devoted to greed, attains the state of a musk-rat.
A man who denies what was deposited in trust, such a dead man is born in a fish's womb.
Reaching a fish's womb, dying, he is born a man; reaching human state, he is born short-lived.
A man who has done sins is born an animal, O Bharata; and they do not know the measure of themselves, nor know dharma at all.
Men who, having done sins, always get rid of them by vows are joined with pleasure and pain and become sick.
Men of sinful conduct, joined with greed and delusion, are born outcast and as barbarians, without doubt.
Those men who avoid sins from birth are healthy, handsome and wealthy.
Women too, doing sin in this way, obtain it; they become wives of these same creatures.
All the faults in taking another's property have been told; this has been said to you by me in brief, blameless one; in another discourse, O Bharata, you will hear more.
This I heard, great king, as Brahma spoke in the midst of the divine sages, and I was asked as it truly is.
I too have told you all of it as it is. Having heard this, great king, always set your mind on dharma.
[Brihaspati] One who has done sinful deeds and come under the sway of unrighteousness, with a mind turned wrong, goes to hell.
One who, having done wrong through delusion, then repents, with the mind composed, should not do the evil again.
As a man rightly confesses his wrong, with a composed mind, so he is freed, like a snake from its old worn-out slough.
Even without giving many kinds of gifts, one with a composed mind, joined to concentration, attains a good end.
I shall tell the gifts, Yudhishthira, by giving which a man, though he has done what should not be done, is joined with dharma.
Of all gifts, food is declared the best; food should be given first by an upright man who desires dharma.
For food is the life of men, and from it a creature is born; the worlds rest on food, so food is revealed.
Gods, sages, ancestors and men praise only food; by giving food, Kaushika gained heaven.
By feeding ten thousand brahmins, O bull among men, a man always devoted to sins is freed from unrighteousness.
A brahmin honoured for the Veda, having gathered food by begging and given it to a brahmin devoted to study, prospers happily here.
A kshatriya who, without harming brahmins and protecting them justly, gives food won by his own might,
to twice-born aged in the Veda, self-controlled and attentive, the righteous one by that removes evil deeds, O Pandava.
A vaishya who gives to the twice-born food from a farming share, purified by the sixth part, is freed from sins.
A shudra who gives the twice-born food earned by hard toil at risk of life is freed from sin.
One who, harmless, earns food by his own strength and gives it to brahmins does not meet hard places.
A man free of greed who gives to the twice-born, aged in the Veda, food gained justly is freed from sin.
Food gives vigour in the world; having given it, a man becomes vigorous, and, following the path of the good, is freed from all sin.
The path made by givers is that by which the wise go; they give life, and the eternal dharma is theirs.
Food justly earned should be given by a man in every state to a worthy recipient, always; for food is the supreme goal.
By giving food a man does not meet hard places; therefore food should be given, free of injustice.
A householder should always try to eat only after feeding a brahmin; a man should make the day fruitful by giving food.
A man who has fed a thousand brahmins learned in the Veda, in justice, dharma and the histories, O king,
does not go to dreadful hell and does not meet rebirths; joined with all desires, he enjoys the fruit after death.
Thus, joined with happiness, he rejoices free of fever, and is born handsome, renowned and wealthy.
All this has been told to you, the great fruit of giving food; this is the root of dharma and of giving, O Bharata.
[Brihaspati] These are all separate doors of dharma, in all respects; hear them as they are told, six in number, O best of the Bharatas.
Come, I shall tell the supreme highest good of a creature: the dharma based on non-harm, which a man accomplishes.
A man who always keeps three faults in check regarding all beings, and restrains desire and anger, then attains perfection.
One who strikes with the rod beings that do no harm, seeking his own happiness, will not be happy after death.
The man who regards all beings as himself, laying down the rod and conquering anger, prospers happily after death.
Even the gods are bewildered on the path of one who is the self of all beings and sees all beings, seeking the footprints of the footless.
One should not do to another what is disagreeable to oneself. This is dharma in brief; other conduct arises from desire.
In refusal and in giving, in pleasure and pain, in the agreeable and disagreeable, a man attains composure by taking himself as the measure.
[Vaishampayana] Having spoken so to King Yudhishthira, the teacher of the gods, the wise one, went up to heaven as we watched.
Sages, brahmins and gods, O wise one, praise non-harm as the mark of dharma, since the Veda is seen as authority.
O best of kings, a man who does harm by deed, word and mind, how is he freed from suffering?
[Bhishma] This non-harm is declared by the knowers of Brahman to be of four kinds; if even one is lost, it does not stand, O slayer of foes.
As a four-footed creature does not stand on three feet, so, O king, this is said to rest on three causes.
As the footprints of other walkers are all covered in the elephant's footprint, so among the worlds non-harm is declared by dharma to be supreme.
A creature is stained by deed, by word and by mind.
Having first renounced by mind, then by word and deed, the three causes are declared and heard from the knowers of Brahman.
Faults rest in mind, in speech and in taste; therefore wise ascetics do not eat meat.
Thus, great king, this non-harm, fenced by four causes, has been explained to you, and it holds all dharma and wealth.
[Yudhishthira] You earlier spoke of the rule of the shraddha with many kinds of meat; without killing, how can there be meat? This seems contradictory.
Doubt has arisen in us about dharma in giving up meat: what fault is there in eating, and what merit in not eating?
For one who kills and eats, or eats what has been brought by another, or who kills for another's sake, or buys and eats,
I wish to hear this in truth from you, blameless one, so that I may resolve to follow this eternal dharma.
How does one obtain long life, how become strong, how come to be free of defects, and how be born with good marks?
[Bhishma] Hear from me truly, O king, O best of the Kurus, what unrighteousness there is in eating meat, and what its best rule is.
Men desiring beauty, soundness of limb, long life, intelligence, strength and memory, if self-perfected, must avoid harm.
On this there was often a dialogue of the sages, O best of the Kurus; hear their view, Yudhishthira.
One who sacrifices with the Ashvamedha every month for a hundred years, and one who does not eat meat, are equal, in my view.
By abstaining from honey and meat one sacrifices always with the long sacrifice, gives always, and is always an ascetic.
All the Vedas and all sacrifices, O Bharata, would not do that, for one who, having eaten meat, afterwards turns back.
It is hard for one who knows taste to give up meat; but this is the best vow, which gives fearlessness to all beings.
The wise man who gives fearlessness as a gift to all beings becomes in the world a giver of lives, without doubt.
So the wise praise the highest dharma: as one's own life is dear to oneself, so it is to other beings.
The wise and great-souled should reason by taking themselves as measure: even the learned who desire well-being fear death.
What then of those being killed by force, desiring life, healthy and sinless, by sinners who live on meat?
Therefore know, great king, that giving up meat is the best abode of dharma, of heaven and of happiness.
Non-harm is the highest dharma, non-harm is the highest austerity, non-harm is the highest truth; from it dharma proceeds.
Meat does not come from grass, wood or stone; it comes from killing a creature, and so there is fault in eating it.
The gods eat svaha and svadha, and love truth and honesty; know that the flesh-eaters are rakshasas, devoted to crookedness and falsehood.
In forests and terrible places, in hard and thick places, by night and day, at twilights, at crossroads and in assemblies, for one who does not eat meat, O king, fear does not come at the end.
If there were no eater, there would be no killer; the killer kills for the eater's sake.
This is not to be eaten, thus harm is turned away; so killing of deer and others goes on for the eater's sake.
Seeing him turn back, he followed behind with folded hands; the king, Avikshita's son, went to learn from Samvarta.
When the blessed Vyasa had gone, Pandu's son the king, bowed, spoke slowly to his aged father, as if hesitantly.
[Vasudeva] Always you, tiger of the Kurus, and my son Krishna, you two were the mouth of the Vrishni destruction, Dhananjaya.
Both Virata and Drupada, and Dhrishtaketu, O king, Nishatha, Akrura, Samba, Bhanu, Kampa, Vidura-ratha,
